summary:
Count beats up to time x with inclusion–exclusion: x/a + x/b − x/lcm(a, b) (shared hits are subtracted once).
The count grows with x, so binary-search the smallest x with at least n beats. The answer is at most n · min(a, b),
which bounds the search. O(log(n · min(a, b))).

question.md:
Beats are the positive multiples of a or of b (a common multiple counts once). Return the n-th beat modulo
10⁹ + 7.

- **Shared hits count once:** with a = 2, b = 4, every multiple of 4 is also a multiple of 2.
- **n up to 10⁹** and a, b up to 4 × 10⁴: the answer reaches 4 × 10¹³, so search in 64 bits and take the modulo
  only at the end.
- **The modulo doesn't affect the search**; it's just how the (exact) answer is reported.

think.md:
Take a = 4, b = 6, n = 8. Beats: [4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 18, 20, 24, 28, 30]… (12 and 24 are shared). The 8-th is 24.

How many beats are ≤ x? Multiples of a: ⌊x/a⌋. Multiples of b: ⌊x/b⌋. Shared ones (multiples of lcm(a, b) =
12) were counted twice, so subtract ⌊x/12⌋. This count never decreases as x grows, and the n-th beat is the
first x where it reaches n.

think.caption: Multiples of 4 or 6, each counted once.

Range: the first drummer alone produces n beats by `n × a`, so the answer is at most `n × min(a, b)`.
lcm(a, b) = a × b / gcd(a, b) (up to 1.6 × 10⁹, so compute it in 64 bits).

approaches.title: Merge the two beat sequences

idea.md: Walk both sequences of multiples like merging two sorted lists, taking the smaller next hit each time (advancing both when equal), until n beats are counted.

build: Repeat n times: `beat = min(nextA, nextB)`; advance whichever equals it (both if equal).

lines.text: Each drummer's next hit time (64-bit: hits go up to 4 × 10¹³).
The next beat is the earlier of the two next hits; if both drummers hit then, both advance, so the shared hit counts once.

walk.title: Merge the two drummers' hit times in increasing order, counting a shared hit once, until the n-th beat.

limits.md: Walks every beat up to the n-th. Counting beats up to any x is O(1) with inclusion–exclusion, so the n-th beat can be binary-searched.

approaches.title: Binary search with inclusion–exclusion

idea.md: `lcm = a / gcd(a, b) × b`. Search x in `[1, n × min(a, b)]` for the first x with `x/a + x/b − x/lcm ≥ n`. Return `x mod 10⁹ + 7`.

build: Compute gcd (Euclid) and lcm in 64 bits.

lines.text: Least common multiple: shared hits happen every lcm. Divide before multiplying (a / gcd × b) to keep it small, and keep it in 64 bits.

notes.cpp: `std::gcd` (C++17, in `<numeric>`) computes the greatest common divisor.

lines.text: The faster drummer alone reaches n beats by n × min(a, b), so the answer is at most that (64-bit).
Halve the time range: about 46 steps.
Beats up to mid by inclusion–exclusion. Enough → the n-th beat is ≤ mid.
The exact n-th beat, reported modulo 10⁹ + 7.

walk.title: Binary-search the time x: beats up to x = x/a + x/b − x/lcm (lcm(4, 6) = 12). Find the smallest x with at least n beats.

takeaways.md:
- "n-th element of a merged set of arithmetic sequences" → binary search on the value with an
  inclusion–exclusion count.
- Search with exact 64-bit values; apply a requested modulo only to the final answer.
